## Market justice preferences

The study of attitudes towards allocation of social goods is a central topic in the literature on social justice as well as in welfare state research (@vanoorschot_social_2017; @svallfors_political_2007). On the one hand, the literature on social justice has focused on the moral and ethical principles that guide individuals' beliefs about fairness and justice in society. On the other hand, welfare state research has examined how these beliefs are shaped by institutional arrangements and policy contexts. In this context, most of the research has focused on the study of attitudes towards redistribution, which refers to the transfer of resources from one group to another in order to reduce inequality and promote social welfare. However, there is a growing interest in understanding how individuals perceive the role of markets in the distribution of social goods and services, which is referred to as market justice preferences.

The role of markets in the distribution of social goods has been a topic of debate in the literature on social justice and welfare state research. The term commodification it is used to describe the process by which goods and services that were previously provided as public goods are transformed into commodities that can be bought and sold in the market [@fourcade_moral_2007]. This process has been associated with a shift towards market-oriented policies, which prioritize efficiency and individual choice over social welfare and equity. In this context, market justice preferences refer to individuals' beliefs about the fairness of market-based distribution of social goods and services [@lane_market_1986], such as education, health care, and pensions. 

Regarding the operationalization of market justice preferences, survey research has typically focused on the measurement of attitudes towards the provision of social goods and services based on individuals' ability to pay in different policy domain. This agenda has been developed in the context of the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP), which has included questions on market justice preferences in its surveys on social inequality, in particular related to the justification of access to better education and health care based on individuals' ability to pay [@lindh_public_2015; @immergut_it_2020]. Research is this area has found that market justice preferences are associated with individual-level factors, such as socioeconomic status and political ideology, as well as contextual factors, such as the level of privatization in the provision of social goods and services. However, there is still a need for further research to understand the complex interplay between these factors and how they shape individuals' beliefs about market justice.
